title: Type 1 Diabetes: Insulin Is Never Optional
bottomLine: Type 1 diabetes is absolute insulin deficiency. Basal insulin must not be omitted even when oral intake is poor; illness requires more monitoring, ketone assessment and a sick-day plan because insulin interruption can precipitate DKA quickly.
recognize: Polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss and ketosis can be the first presentation.
Pump interruption can cause rapid insulin deficiency because there is no long-acting depot.
differentiate: Type 2 diabetes can also present with ketosis, especially during severe illness; classification uses clinical context and selected antibody/C-peptide testing when uncertain.
assessment: Review insulin regimen, CGM/pump data, hypoglycemia, ketones, injection sites, eating patterns, exercise and psychosocial burden.
workup: Use A1C and glucose data for chronic control and ketone testing during hyperglycemia/illness; screen for associated autoimmune and microvascular disease according to age/duration guidance.
management: Use individualized basal-bolus or pump therapy, carbohydrate/meal planning and education; ensure access to glucagon and ketone testing.
medicationSafety: Never stop basal insulin in type 1 diabetes because the patient is NPO without a clinician-directed replacement strategy.
counselling: Teach sick-day rules, pump-failure backup and hypoglycemia treatment.
followUp: Use Diabetes Canada current type 1 guidance and interprofessional diabetes support.
examTrap: Holding all insulin when a person with type 1 diabetes is not eating.
oneLinePearl: No food may change insulin dose; it does not remove the need for basal insulin.

title: DKA and HHS: Fluids, Potassium, Insulin, Cause
bottomLine: DKA and HHS are metabolic emergencies requiring protocolized fluids, potassium-aware insulin therapy, frequent monitoring and treatment of the precipitant. Potassium may be depleted even when the initial serum value is normal or high.
recognize: DKA has ketosis and metabolic acidosis; HHS has profound hyperglycemia/hyperosmolality with less ketosis and often severe dehydration.
differentiate: Starvation/alcoholic ketosis and lactic acidosis can mimic parts of DKA; HHS often occurs in older adults with type 2 diabetes.
assessment: Assess volume status, mental status, infection/ischemia, medication adherence, pregnancy and SGLT2-inhibitor use.
workup: Use glucose, electrolytes, bicarbonate/pH, ketones, osmolality, renal function and cause-specific testing.
management: Use a validated acute-care protocol: fluid resuscitation, potassium-guided insulin, dextrose when needed to continue clearing ketosis, and precipitant treatment.
medicationSafety: SGLT2 inhibitors can cause euglycemic DKA; do not rule out DKA because glucose is not extremely high.
counselling: After recovery, review sick-day medication holds, insulin access and why the episode occurred.
followUp: Ensure diabetes follow-up and medication reconciliation before discharge.
examTrap: Starting insulin without knowing the potassium status in severe DKA.
oneLinePearl: DKA treatment is potassium-aware insulin plus fluids and cause control.

title: Hypoglycemia: Treat Now, Then Find Why
bottomLine: Symptomatic hypoglycemia requires immediate glucose treatment; severe hypoglycemia with inability to self-treat requires external rescue. After recovery, identify the cause and reduce recurrence risk.
recognize: Adrenergic symptoms include tremor, sweating and palpitations; neuroglycopenia causes confusion, seizure or coma.
differentiate: Sulfonylurea- or long-acting insulin-associated hypoglycemia can recur after initial correction.
assessment: Confirm glucose when feasible without delaying treatment, and review insulin/secretagogues, meals, exercise, alcohol, CKD, liver disease and adrenal disease.
workup: Persistent unexplained hypoglycemia without diabetes requires a dedicated diagnostic evaluation rather than assuming poor intake.
management: Use fast-acting carbohydrate when conscious and safe to swallow; use glucagon or IV dextrose for severe episodes according to setting.
medicationSafety: Renal impairment increases hypoglycemia risk from insulin and some secretagogues; glyburide is particularly problematic in older adults/CKD.
redFlags: Pregnancy or frailty with severe event
counselling: Teach the 15-minute recheck approach for mild episodes and ensure family/caregivers know rescue glucagon when prescribed.
followUp: Adjust the causative regimen and review CGM/SMBG patterns.
examTrap: Treating the low glucose and sending the patient home without changing the medication that caused it.
oneLinePearl: A corrected glucose ends the episode, not the investigation.

title: Obesity: Treat a Chronic Disease Without Blame
bottomLine: Obesity care should be complication-centred and non-stigmatizing. Assess metabolic, mechanical, mental-health and medication contributors, then use nutrition/activity support, pharmacotherapy and bariatric referral when indicated and desired.
recognize: Complications include diabetes, hypertension, OSA, MASLD, osteoarthritis, infertility and psychosocial harm.
differentiate: BMI is a screening measure, not a complete measure of health or adiposity distribution.
assessment: Ask permission to discuss weight; assess trajectory, comorbidities, eating disorder symptoms, medications, sleep, pregnancy plans, access to food/activity and goals.
workup: Screen for diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension, liver disease and other complications based on risk; do not order broad endocrine testing without clinical suspicion.
management: Use evidence-based behavioural support and anti-obesity medication or metabolic/bariatric surgery pathways when benefits fit patient goals and risks.
medicationSafety: Review contraindications and pregnancy plans for anti-obesity medications; avoid unregulated weight-loss products.
counselling: Use person-centred language and focus on health outcomes rather than moralizing weight.
followUp: Track tolerability, cardiometabolic outcomes, function and goals, not only kilograms lost.
examTrap: Telling a patient with severe obesity and complications simply to diet and exercise before offering evidence-based treatment.
oneLinePearl: Obesity treatment is chronic disease care, not a motivation test.

title: Thyroid Nodule: Ultrasound Risk Before Biopsy
bottomLine: A thyroid nodule needs TSH plus risk-based ultrasound assessment. Biopsy depends on sonographic risk and size, not on palpability alone.
recognize: Concerning features include rapid growth, hard/fixed nodule, cervical nodes, hoarseness, radiation exposure or strong family history.
differentiate: A suppressed TSH suggests an autonomously functioning nodule and changes the workup; most nodules are benign.
assessment: Assess compressive symptoms, voice change, thyroid symptoms, radiation/family history and cervical nodes.
workup: Order TSH and thyroid ultrasound; use fine-needle aspiration according to accepted ultrasound risk criteria.
management: Refer suspicious nodules/cytology and manage functional nodules according to thyroid status and specialist pathway.
medicationSafety: Do not use levothyroxine suppression therapy routinely for benign nodules because harms can exceed benefit.
counselling: Explain that surveillance is appropriate for many low-risk nodules.
followUp: Repeat ultrasound only at intervals justified by risk and prior results.
examTrap: Biopsying every incidentally detected thyroid nodule.
oneLinePearl: Nodule biopsy is ultrasound-risk driven, not fear driven.

title: Hyperthyroidism: Recognize Thyroid Storm
bottomLine: Hyperthyroidism causes adrenergic symptoms, weight loss and cardiovascular complications; fever, marked tachyarrhythmia, CNS change or heart failure with thyrotoxicosis may be thyroid storm and requires emergency multidrug treatment.
recognize: Graves disease may cause diffuse goitre and eye findings; older adults may present with atrial fibrillation or apathy rather than tremor.
differentiate: Thyroiditis causes hormone release but does not respond to antithyroid drugs the same way as Graves/toxic nodules.
assessment: Assess HR/rhythm, heart failure, eye symptoms, goitre/nodules, pregnancy, medication/iodine exposure and precipitating infection.
workup: TSH with free thyroid hormones confirms thyrotoxicosis; antibodies and imaging distinguish cause when needed.
management: Treat routine hyperthyroidism by cause; thyroid storm requires emergency beta blockade when appropriate, antithyroid medication, iodine sequencing, corticosteroid and precipitant treatment under acute-care guidance.
medicationSafety: Antithyroid drugs can cause agranulocytosis and hepatotoxicity; fever/sore throat requires urgent CBC assessment.
counselling: Teach medication toxicity warning signs and smoking cessation for thyroid eye disease.
followUp: Trend thyroid function and definitive-treatment plan.
examTrap: Treating thyroiditis with escalating antithyroid medication without establishing the cause of thyrotoxicosis.
oneLinePearl: Thyrotoxicosis is the state; the cause determines the treatment.
sourceBasis: Canadian Society of Endocrinology and Metabolism practice resources

title: Hypothyroidism: Routine Replacement vs Myxedema Emergency
bottomLine: Primary hypothyroidism is usually managed with levothyroxine titrated to TSH, but hypothermia, bradycardia, hypoventilation and altered consciousness can signal myxedema coma and require emergency care.
recognize: Fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, weight gain and menstrual change are common but nonspecific.
differentiate: Central hypothyroidism may have an inappropriately normal/low TSH and requires free T4 interpretation plus pituitary evaluation.
assessment: Review symptoms, pregnancy, cardiac disease, medications/supplements and adherence/timing relative to food/iron/calcium.
workup: Use TSH and free T4 appropriately; thyroid antibodies can support autoimmune etiology but need not be repeated serially.
management: Use levothyroxine replacement with cautious initiation in frail patients or significant coronary disease; myxedema coma requires ICU-level thyroid hormone and adrenal coverage.
medicationSafety: Iron, calcium and some medications impair levothyroxine absorption; biotin can interfere with thyroid assays.
counselling: Explain consistent dosing and separation from interfering supplements.
followUp: Recheck thyroid function after meaningful dose changes and more promptly in pregnancy.
examTrap: Increasing levothyroxine because of a single abnormal TSH without checking adherence and administration timing.
oneLinePearl: Before changing the dose, check how the levothyroxine is actually being taken.
sourceBasis: Canadian Society of Endocrinology and Metabolism resources

title: Cushing Syndrome: Screen Only When the Phenotype Fits
bottomLine: Cushing syndrome should be tested when there are multiple progressive or discriminatory features, not for uncomplicated obesity alone. Exogenous glucocorticoid exposure is the first cause to exclude.
recognize: Easy bruising, proximal weakness, wide violaceous striae, facial plethora, osteoporosis, difficult hypertension/diabetes and growth deceleration in children are more specific clues.
differentiate: Common obesity, depression and alcohol use can mimic some features; pseudo-Cushing states require careful interpretation.
assessment: Review all steroid exposure including inhaled, injected, topical and supplements before endocrine testing.
workup: Use validated first-line cortisol screening tests and confirm abnormal results before localizing the source.
management: Refer confirmed endogenous hypercortisolism to endocrinology; taper exogenous steroids safely when possible rather than abruptly stopping chronic therapy.
medicationSafety: Chronic glucocorticoids suppress the HPA axis and abrupt cessation can precipitate adrenal crisis.
counselling: Explain steroid sick-day and taper plans when HPA suppression is possible.
followUp: Monitor metabolic, bone and cardiovascular complications.
examTrap: Ordering cortisol screening solely because a patient has obesity and hypertension.
oneLinePearl: Cushing testing needs a Cushing phenotype; first ask about steroids.

title: Pituitary Mass and Hyperprolactinemia: Medication or Compression?
bottomLine: Hyperprolactinemia can be medication-related, physiologic, hypothyroid or pituitary. Visual symptoms or sudden severe headache with pituitary disease are urgent because mass effect or apoplexy can threaten vision and life.
recognize: Galactorrhea, amenorrhea, infertility, sexual dysfunction or hypogonadism can occur; large masses can cause bitemporal visual loss.
differentiate: Antipsychotics and other dopamine-blocking drugs are common causes; pregnancy and hypothyroidism must be considered before assuming prolactinoma.
assessment: Review pregnancy possibility, medications, headaches, vision, menstrual/sexual history and thyroid symptoms.
workup: Repeat/confirm prolactin when appropriate, check pregnancy/TSH, and use pituitary MRI when persistent unexplained elevation or mass symptoms justify it.
management: Treat prolactinoma with specialist-guided dopamine agonist therapy in most cases; urgent endocrine/neurosurgical care for apoplexy or significant compression.
medicationSafety: Do not abruptly stop an effective antipsychotic solely to normalize prolactin without psychiatric risk-benefit planning.
counselling: Discuss fertility implications and medication tradeoffs.
followUp: Monitor prolactin, symptoms and imaging according to diagnosis.
examTrap: Calling elevated prolactin a pituitary tumour before reviewing antipsychotic medication and pregnancy status.
oneLinePearl: Before MRI for prolactin, check pregnancy, thyroid and medications.

title: SIADH and Diabetes Insipidus: Concentrated vs Dilute Urine
bottomLine: SIADH causes inappropriate water retention with hypotonic hyponatremia and inappropriately concentrated urine; diabetes insipidus causes inability to conserve water, producing high-volume dilute urine and hypernatremia risk.
recognize: SIADH triggers include CNS/pulmonary disease and medications; DI follows pituitary injury or nephrogenic causes such as lithium.
differentiate: Primary polydipsia also causes dilute urine but has different serum tonicity and diagnostic response patterns.
assessment: Assess fluid balance, neurologic symptoms, urine volume, thirst, medications, CNS history and volume status.
workup: Pair serum and urine osmolality/sodium; use specialist-directed water-deprivation/copeptin strategies when DI type remains uncertain.
management: Treat symptomatic severe hyponatremia urgently; otherwise manage SIADH with cause-directed therapy and fluid strategy.
Central DI generally responds to desmopressin; nephrogenic DI requires cause-specific measures.
medicationSafety: Desmopressin over-treatment can cause dangerous hyponatremia; lithium can cause nephrogenic DI.
counselling: Teach fluid and medication instructions precisely.
followUp: Trend sodium and osmolality during therapy changes.
examTrap: Giving unrestricted free water to every sodium disorder without first identifying the physiology.
oneLinePearl: SIADH holds water; DI loses water.

title: Osteoporosis: Fracture Risk Beyond the T-Score
bottomLine: Osteoporosis treatment decisions incorporate fragility fracture history and absolute fracture risk, not DXA T-score alone. A hip or vertebral fragility fracture is high-risk disease even if the T-score is not below -2.5.
recognize: Risk rises with age, prior fragility fracture, glucocorticoids, low body weight, smoking, falls and secondary bone disease.
differentiate: Osteomalacia and metastatic bone disease cause bone symptoms through different mechanisms and require different testing.
assessment: Ask prior fractures, falls, steroids, menopause/hypogonadism, calcium/vitamin D intake, renal/GI/endocrine disease and dental plans.
workup: Use DXA and a validated Canadian fracture-risk approach; evaluate secondary causes when indicated.
management: Use fall prevention, adequate nutrition/activity and anti-osteoporosis medication based on fracture risk; very high risk may warrant anabolic therapy/specialist care.
medicationSafety: Bisphosphonate use requires renal and GI considerations; denosumab should not be stopped without a transition plan because rebound vertebral fractures can occur.
counselling: Discuss rare medication adverse effects in proportion to much larger fracture-prevention benefits.
followUp: Monitor adherence, fractures and treatment duration/transition rather than repeating DXA excessively.
examTrap: Withholding treatment after a low-trauma hip fracture because the T-score is -2.0.
oneLinePearl: A fragility fracture can diagnose high fracture risk even without an osteoporotic T-score.

title: MASLD: Cardiometabolic Liver Disease Needs Fibrosis Risk Stratification
bottomLine: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease is common in diabetes and obesity, but the key prognostic question is fibrosis risk. Normal or mildly elevated aminotransferases do not exclude advanced fibrosis.
recognize: Risk rises with type 2 diabetes, central adiposity, dyslipidemia and hypertension.
differentiate: Exclude significant alcohol exposure, viral hepatitis and medication/other liver causes when the pattern is not clearly metabolic.
assessment: Assess cardiometabolic risk, alcohol, medications and signs of chronic liver disease.
workup: Use non-invasive fibrosis risk stratification such as FIB-4 followed by elastography/specialist pathway when elevated or indeterminate.
management: Prioritize weight and cardiometabolic treatment with therapies that also improve cardiovascular/renal outcomes when indicated; refer advanced fibrosis/cirrhosis.
medicationSafety: Do not avoid indicated statins solely because of uncomplicated stable MASLD.
counselling: Frame liver risk as part of metabolic health and avoid blame-based counselling.
followUp: Reassess fibrosis risk and metabolic disease over time.
examTrap: Using normal ALT to rule out clinically important fibrotic liver disease.
oneLinePearl: In MASLD, fibrosis stage predicts outcome better than ALT.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association for the Study of the Liver resources
